svg.aria-label: Diagram: three levels of read-model separation on AWS and what each one costs. The first is a global secondary index, which is CQRS already built: the index holds a selection of attributes organised by a different key, DynamoDB updates it asynchronously using an eventually consistent model, applications never write directly to it, and its provisioned throughput settings are separate from the base table's. Its limits are listed: GetItem and BatchGetItem cannot be used on it, queries cannot fetch attributes from the base table so the projection is the contract, it only tracks items whose key attributes actually exist so it is sparse, and query results are capped at one megabyte. The second level is a hand-built read model fed by a change stream, which is needed when the query shape is one an index cannot serve, such as full text search or aggregation or a join, and which costs a projector to write, deploy and monitor. A panel records the finding that matters most for provisioning: the coupling runs backwards from what people expect, because AWS states that if a global secondary index has insufficient write capacity the write activity on the table will be throttled, and that for a table write to succeed the table and all of its indexes must have enough write capacity or the write is throttled. The guidance is therefore to provision index write capacity equal to or greater than the base table's. A final panel records the write amplification rules: changing an indexed key attribute costs two writes, one to delete the old index entry and one to put the new one, while an update touching neither index keys nor projected attributes consumes no index capacity though the base table is still charged.
svg.title: The index is already a read model, and it can throttle the writes
svg.text: Most teams considering CQRS are describing an index with extra steps
Asynchronous projection, separate key, separate capacity, eventual consistency — already running.
Rung 1 · Global secondary index
CQRS you already have. No projector to own.
• Updated “asynchronously, using an eventually
consistent model”
• “Applications never write directly to an index”
• Throughput settings separate from the table
What it cannot do
No GetItem or BatchGetItem · cannot fetch from the
base table · sparse by design · 1 MB query cap
Rung 2 · Hand-built read model
A stream, a projector, a second store.
Earned by a named requirement:
• full-text search
• arbitrary aggregation
• joins across entities
What it costs
A component that can fail on its own, and a lag
usually longer than the index’s fraction of a second.
The coupling runs backwards from what everyone expects
“If you perform heavy write activity on the table, but a global secondary index on that table has insufficient write
capacity, the write activity on the table will be throttled.”
The read model does not quietly fall behind — it stops the writes. Provision index write capacity at or above the table’s.
Write amplification is per-attribute, not per-write
Changing an indexed key attribute: two writes — one to delete the old index entry, one to put the new one.
Changing an attribute that is neither an index key nor projected: no index capacity at all (the table is still charged).
Index the attributes that are queried, not the ones that change. A status field used as an index key is the expensive one.
And if a read must reflect a write, no read model satisfies it — read the table, strongly consistent, which an index cannot offer.
